I study how climate shapes the growth, function, and survival of trees — from the
slow pressure of shifting averages to the sharp blows of drought and heat, and
the long shadow these leave behind. My work combines ecological and climate
time-series analysis, statistical and machine-learning models, and
dynamical-systems thinking, drawing on dendrometer records, flux-tower data,
global tree-ring archives, and high-resolution climate datasets.

Across projects, a single question recurs: how does a changing climate reshape
the long-term trajectory of tree growth, function, and survival? I approach it
from several directions at once — data-driven, mechanistic, and instrumental —
because the answer lives at the intersection of all three.

---

## Disentangling soil and atmospheric drought

Drought is not one thing. Trees experience it both through the soil (falling
water availability at the roots) and through the atmosphere (rising vapor
pressure deficit that pulls water from the canopy). These pressures usually
arrive together, which makes their separate effects hard to disentangle — yet
they act on the tree through different mechanisms.

In a semi-arid pine forest, I used high-resolution dendrometer measurements
together with an irrigation experiment — where relieving soil drought isolates
the effect of atmospheric drought — to separate how each shapes the daily cycles
of stem growth, contraction, and recovery. A central result: heatwaves
consistently depress stem expansion, but the consequence depends on soil water.
Trees with a soil-water buffer merely slow down, while trees already at the edge
are pushed into net contraction — losing water and shrinking rather than growing.

This is the first published chapter of my PhD.

[Read the manuscript &#8594;](files/Feuer-etal-2025-PCE-tree-growth-drought.pdf)

## Losses outlast gains: a century of tree growth under climate change

Under climate change, will forests grow more or less? The answer differs from
place to place, which has long obscured the overall direction. To trace it, we
learned nonlinear climate–growth relationships from 4,110 Northern Hemisphere
tree-ring chronologies recorded since 1902 — more than 12 million ring-width
measurements — and projected them through the twenty-first century under CMIP6
climate scenarios.

Two findings stand out:

- Across the Northern Hemisphere, projected growth declines, driven by warming
  and rising atmospheric water demand whose negative effect outweighs the gains
  from changing precipitation.
- The response is asymmetric in time: once losses emerge they are rarely
  reversed, whereas gains tend to fade. The pattern holds in every well-sampled
  region and strengthens under stronger warming, with the sharpest declines in
  the Mediterranean and western and central Europe.

Growth does not simply move back and forth between good years and bad — it is
pulled in one direction.

[Read the manuscript &#8594;](files/Feuer-etal-losses-outlast-gains.pdf)

## Where the tree-ring record can speak for a changing climate

The International Tree-Ring Data Bank is the largest archive of tree-ring records
on Earth, and it underpins much of what we know about how forests respond to
climate. But it was never designed as a climatic sample: some climates are
densely represented, others barely at all. This project asks how well the record
covers the climates trees actually experience, and how that coverage shifts as
the climate warms.

Two ideas sit at its core. The first is space-for-time substitution — the common
assumption that spatial climate gradients can stand in for change over time, that
a warmer place tells us about a warmer future; I examine how far that holds across
the network, where places are interchangeable and where they are not. The second
is novel climates: as warming pushes forests toward conditions with no analog in
the existing record, parts of the world move outside the sampled envelope.
Mapping where coverage is dense versus sparse shows where the record can support
confident inference, and where new sampling would most improve our ability to
anticipate how forests respond.

## Drought history reshapes tree survival under recurrent water stress

I am developing a minimal dynamical-systems model of tree carbon and hydraulic
function to explore how drought history changes the response to future stress. A
drought can leave a tree alive but physiologically displaced: hydraulic damage,
carbon depletion, and structural changes may persist long after environmental
conditions recover. A subsequent drought therefore acts on a different state of
the system. The project asks when successive events buffer one another, when they
amplify one another, and when incomplete recovery pushes a tree across the
boundary between recovery and mortality.

The dynamical-systems picture is the heart of it. Picture a plane whose axes are
the tree's carbon reserves and its hydraulic function. A healthy, self-restoring
state sits in one corner, separated by a threshold — a separatrix — from states
that slide toward mortality. A drought temporarily bends the flow and displaces
the tree; when it ends, the tree begins to recover, but from wherever the drought
left it. A second drought that would have been survivable from full health can,
arriving before recovery is complete, carry the tree across the threshold.

The key idea is that disturbance history matters beyond cumulative severity: two
drought sequences with similar total exposure can end very differently depending
on how intense, how long, and how closely spaced the events are.

---

## Future directions

My longer-term interest is the mechanistic basis of tree growth and mortality
under climate change — how the twin currencies of tree health, carbon and water,
are drawn down as the climate shifts, and how that determines which trees recover
and which cross the line into decline.

I want to keep working across scales and methods: from individual-tree physiology
measured at high resolution, to continental patterns in the tree-ring record, to
mechanistic models that tie the two together. The unifying goal is to understand,
and eventually forecast, forest resilience and vulnerability — not just how trees
respond to the climate they have known, but how they will fare in the climates
they are about to meet.

I am seeking postdoc opportunities beginning fall 2027, and I welcome
conversations about projects and collaborations along these lines.
